 Features How childhood fascination and family prayers fuelled Ashrifah’s golden journey 
 19 November 2026 Hangzhou (China) Real name : Priyanka Sharma Nurisa Dian Ashrifah was just 11 years old when she watched The Hunger Games , the popular dystopian film series based on Suzanne Collins’ novels, and thought its bow-wielding heroine, Katniss Everdeen, was “really cool”. 
 Little did she know that her fascination with the fictional character would one day lead her to the top of an Asian Games podium. 
 As luck would have it, her school had just introduced archery as an extracurricular activity. Ashrifah signed up, picked up a bow and soon developed a passion for the sport. 
 Nine years later, the 20-year-old Indonesian made history at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games , winning her country’s first-ever archery gold medal at the continental event . And she did it in style. 
 Following her Asian Games triumph, Ashrifah returned to international competition at the Hangzhou 2026 Asia Cup this week. After qualifying second with 706 points , she reached the quarterfinals of the compound women’s individual event, where she was beaten 146-142 by India’s Prithika Pradeep . 
 Competing in her first Asian Games, Ashrifah overcame some of the world’s leading compound archers, including India’s top seed Chikitha Taniparthi and Korea’s teenage sensation Kang Yeonseo , before defeating the Philippines’ Amaya Amparo Cojuangco 139-137 in the compound women’s individual final. 
 For someone who had arrived at the Games with few expectations, standing on the top step of the podium was almost surreal. 
 “I used to only imagine what it would feel like to be here, and I never truly expected that I would actually make it,” said Ashrifah, who was ranked 31st at the time. “The journey to this moment involved many challenges, and not all of them were easy.” 
 “But today, I am grateful, because every step of that process led me to this very moment. And we finally made it.” 
 The victory was not just a personal breakthrough. It was a historic moment for Indonesian archery. 
 “This victory means so much, not only to me personally but also to my country,” she said. “I hope this achievement can make Indonesia proud and inspire the next generation of Indonesian archers to dream even bigger.” 
 Ashrifah began training seriously at 13 and gradually gained experience competing in national tournaments. 
 Her international debut came only in 2025, when she represented Indonesia at the World Archery Championships in Gwangju . 
 She returned from Korea without a medal but with valuable lessons, which she put to good use at the 2025 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games in Thailand, where she claimed three medals, including the compound women’s individual and team titles. 
 Less than a year later, she was preparing for the biggest competition of her career. 
 Training for Aichi-Nagoya 2026 began in February, when she joined the national training centre in Jakarta. However, a decentralised training programme between March and June meant she had to adapt her preparation. 
 During that period, she trained at her home in Semarang, the capital of Indonesia’s Central Java province, and relied largely on online communication with her coaches. 
 “I initially struggled a little to get my performance back to where it was before,” she recalled. 
 “Fortunately, it didn’t take too long for me to readjust, regain my rhythm, and get back to my usual performance.” 
 During that period, Ashrifah drew strength from the people closest to her. 
 “Thank you so much to my mother and my brother for your constant prayers and support, which have been with me all along. Thank you to my coaches for your patience and for guiding me to this point.” 
 Ashrifah arrived at the Asian Games without expecting to win a medal , knowing that she would be up against archers from powerhouse nations such as India and Korea. 
 That approach helped her overcome higher-ranked opponents, including Taniparthi in the quarterfinals and Yeonseo in the semifinals. 
 “I simply focused on my technique, trying to shoot smoothly, comfortably, and consistently, and let the results take care of themselves,” she explained. 
 But reaching the final brought a different feeling. 
 “It was only when I reached the final that I started getting really excited and eager to win,” she admitted. “Maybe I was a little too overwhelmed by that excitement, which affected my performance and scoring in the final.” 
 Despite the nerves, Ashrifah held her composure to edge Cojuangco 139-137 and complete her remarkable run. 
 She said her historic victory had taught her important lessons about “confidence and perseverance”. 
 “Never underestimate yourself just because your opponent is ranked higher than you,” she said. “You never know what might happen. So keep pushing yourself, keep believing, and always give your best.” 
 Irawadi Dermadharana , secretary general of the Indonesian Archery Association, praised the youngster, saying that Ashrifah’s achievement could mark a turning point for the sport in the country. 
 “This gold medal is a historic milestone for Indonesian archery,” Dermadharana said. “This achievement means a great deal to our nation, our federation, and the entire archery community. 
 “Beyond the medal itself, this victory represents the results of years of hard work, dedication, and commitment from our athletes, coaches, officials, and everyone involved in Indonesian archery.” 
 The federation is now looking to build on that success in the build-up to the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games . 
 “Looking ahead to the LA28 Games, our federation is committed to strengthening our athlete development programmes, improving coaching quality, expanding international competition exposure, and providing better technical and performance support,” Dermadharana added. 
 “We hope this historic achievement will encourage more young Indonesians to take up archery and become part of the future of our sport.” 
 For Ashrifah, the next big dream is already taking shape. 
 With compound archery set to make its Olympic debut in the mixed team event at LA28, she hopes to earn a place in the Indonesian team.
 “Qualifying for the LA28 Olympics and having the opportunity to compete there is something I really dream of,” she said. 
 “I would be incredibly proud, happy, and grateful if I could bring home another medal from the Olympics and once again make Indonesia proud.” 
 As she celebrates the biggest achievement of her career, Ashrifah hopes her journey will inspire a new generation of Indonesian archers to follow their dreams.
